slides.text: When I testified against the Russo crime family, the FBI relocated me to a sleepy town in Vermont and gave me a rusty food truck as a front. My handler’s only rule was simple: 'Make the food so aggressively mediocre that nobody ever talks about you.' So on opening day, I panicked and served cold unseasoned radish slices on burnt toast with a single drop of balsamic vinegar, charging twenty-eight dollars so locals would stay away.

Unfortunately, a weekend food critic from Manhattan wandered by, took one bite, and burst into tears. Next Monday, the New York Times called my burnt toast 'a brutalist, post-ironic triumph of culinary minimalism.' Within forty-eight hours, tech billionaires and French sommeliers were camping outside my truck in sleeping bags, begging me to insult them while handing them raw turnips.

Yesterday, Don Russo’s deadliest hitman showed up at the window. I reached for my frying pan, ready to die. Instead, the hitman slid a hundred-dollar bill across the counter and whispered, 'Don Russo knows who you are, Frankie. And if you don't get him a table for four before the Michelin inspectors arrive on Friday, you're a dead man.' I sighed and penciled the mafia in for 7:30.
